test_title: SSC MTS (2022) Official Paper (Held On: 10 May, 2023 Shift 3)
subject: general
question:
The statement below has been given with bracketed text. Select the option with correct Idiom for the bracketed text.

Susie (has such strong resemblance to) Kate Winslet that sometimes people would ask her for her autograph
solution:
The correct answer is **"dead ringer".**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **"Dead ringer" **is an idiom that perfectly fits the context of the statement about Susie and Kate Winslet. This phrase is commonly used to indicate a person or thing strongly resembling another.
 
• "Dead ringer" is an idiomatic expression that refers to someone who looks very similar to another person. It implies a remarkable resemblance, often to the point where the two individuals could be mistaken for each other. 
 
• The context does not discuss insanity, multiple multitasking ability, or the act of searching for work rigorously, which are the meanings conveyed by other idiomatic expressions provided as options.
 
• The idiom **"dead ringer" **signifies an exact physical similarity between two people, which is why people sometimes ask Susie for her autograph, mistaking her for Kate Winslet.

Therefore, the correct answer is **"Option 1".**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• The idiom "dead ringer" originated in the the US, and its first usage in the sense of being an exact duplicate can be traced back to the late 19th to early 20th century. It's interesting to note that earlier, the term "ringer" was used in horse racing to refer to a horse substituted for another in order to fraudulently win a race. Later, "dead" was added as an intensifier to mean 'absolute' or 'exact' referred to exact duplicity or similarity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **"Gone bananas": **This phrase generally means to go crazy or irrational. It has no contextual relevance here.
 
• **"Jack of all trades": **This expression refers to a person who is competent in many skills but not necessarily outstanding in any. It doesn't apply in the context of resembling a celebrity.
 
• **"Pound the pavement": **Typically meaning to walk the streets in search for employment or as part of work. As it doesn't convey any sense of physical resemblance or similarity, it's not applicable here.
